transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Sorry, I'm a couple minutes late. Where are you all at? I was hoping we could at least nail down the student-facing hint behavior today, and what evidence we need from the pilot, before I get too concrete with the configuration.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: We’ve really only just started, so good timing. I’d strongly prefer graduated hints, where students have enough space to try a strategy before the tutor gets more explicit, and then weekly paper exit tickets so we can see whether the reasoning carries beyond the interface. The key practical piece is, um, stable de-identified IDs in the session logs from week one. Otherwise we can’t connect those two sources.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: That linkage is the dependency on my side too. I can configure a genuinely graduated policy, first a strategic prompt, then a more targeted step, with a worked answer only after explicit escalation. But before I commit, Elena, how comparable do you expect those weekly exit tickets- if the three classes are pacing a little differently, how comparable do you expect them to be?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: They should be comparable enough if we anchor them to the same underlying algebraic idea, instead of insisting on identical items every Friday. I'd want one or two common prompts that ask for a step and an explanation, so we can tell the difference between a student who gets an answer and one who can articulate the strategy. I do need to check the timing though- against each teacher's April sequence first.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: That works for the linkage, as long as we keep the underlying concept tag and the form of each common prompt. I don't need identical items to join the records. I'll need to confirm Ridgeway's roster-to-anonymous-ID procedure and make sure the export actually starts in week one, but then we can keep the telemetry de-identified and still align tutor behavior with the exit-ticket construct.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: And I’d be careful not to read the linked traces as effort scores on their own. A student taking a hint—or taking a long time after one—might be checking their reasoning, might be stuck, or might just have been pulled away. Arun, does the event stream let us tell sustained hint reading from, um, device-idle time, or do those collapse into the same latency?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: They don't have to collapse. I can log focus and visibility transitions, along with whether the hint panel was actually open, so we can separate a likely device-idle interval from time when the hint was rendered. Though rendered is not the same as read, obviously. I wouldn't put either measure into a teacher flag on its own. The useful unit may be a pattern across the problem flow.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: That’s exactly why I’d want the paper work alongside it. A sparse trace, or a long pause, doesn’t tell us whether the student was reasoning productively. I saw that just last week, a student could explain an equation strategy aloud and then leave half the intermediate steps off the page. Arun, when you flag a session, what would the teacher actually see? The problem and hint sequence, or just a label?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: I’d make the default a compact case card, not just a bare label. It would show the problem’s concept tag, the hint stages shown, a small response timeline, and the specific reason it was surfaced. The underlying event trace can still be available for audit, but I don’t want teachers having to interpret raw clicks. And I’d only surface a flag when there’s a defined pattern, not, say, three retries in isolation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: That sounds usable, especially if the card opens on the actual student response and not just the timeline. Otherwise the teacher is still being asked to infer too much. I’d keep it strictly optional in this six-week April pilot, though. We shouldn’t create a weekly review task and then call it, um, ordinary classroom use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Keeping it optional is important, and I’d avoid calling these “flags” in the teacher view, if we can. Maybe they’re just sessions to review, with the stated reason and the student’s actual work, because a pattern is a prompt for- it gives you context, not evidence that the student is off-task or disengaged.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: “Sessions to review” is better. I can make the reason operational but non-diagnostic, something like repeated answer escalation with subsequent incorrect attempts, alongside the response history and the actual work, rather than infer disengagement. And Elena, I can include the student response in the card. Would teachers want the full, full text by default, or just the most recent attempt with an expand control?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Most recent attempt with an expand control, I think. In a normal week, that gives a teacher enough to decide whether it's worth looking, without dropping a wall of text on them. But the full exchange needs to be there when they expand it because the wording of the student's, um, reasoning is often the whole story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, that feels lighter.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Good. I’ll keep the card collapsed to the latest attempt, with the full exchange behind expand, and make the review queue opt-in instead of pushing it into a teacher’s weekly workflow. One thing I want to sanity-check with Nia, though, is for a review trigger, what combination of answer requests and subsequent attempts would still feel like ordinary strategic checking rather than—what would be worth surfacing?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: I wouldn't set a numeric rule based just on answer requests. In our short study, high-confidence students often used optional hints to verify a line of reasoning, so I'd only surface it when the escalation is followed by, say, repeated incompatible attempts or a clear shift away from the strategy the student had been using. Or rather, even then, it should be a review prompt, not a concern label.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: That is implementable, although “incompatible” needs a computable proxy. We could define it against the problem’s expected intermediate state, or against a contradiction with the student’s immediately prior strategy, and then have the card say exactly which transition triggered review. I’d want to inspect a few real April traces before fixing any threshold, though. The dry run had that odd answer-request- then-more-attempts pattern, and I do not yet know whether that is confusion or just the interface.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: I think that’s the right place to be cautious. Before we make a proxy do too much, could we look at a small set of those dry-run sequences with what the student actually entered and, if possible, ask a few students what they thought they were doing? The same transition could be a misconception, or, I mean, it could be them testing an alternative after the tutor’s wording.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Oh, that would be useful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: I can pull a purposive sample of those sequences with the prompt, each student entry, hint state, and focus events, without exposing identity. If we do brief student recall conversations, I’d rather use the trace as a memory cue than ask them to interpret a label we’ve already assigned. That may tell us whether the behavior is a UI artifact, or I should say an interface artifact, before we encode it as a review rule.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Using the trace as a recall cue is much better. I do need to look at the wording and timing for those conversations, and any very brief motivation items, so seventh graders aren’t being asked to explain themselves in a way that feels evaluative or interrupts the math period. But a small, varied sample could tell us a lot about whether the escalation feels supportive or kind of...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Hm, yes, carefully.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: For those recall conversations, I'd want us to recruit across different trace patterns, not just the sequences we think look concerning. And the paper exit ticket from that same week could be a useful third piece of context too. Assuming Ridgeway can give us the stable anonymous ID linkage beginning in the first week of April- assuming we have that linkage.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Sampling across the trace distribution matters. Otherwise we train ourselves to see the behavior only as a defect. Technically, I can select a small stratified set with answer escalation and retries, hint-only use, long apparent idle intervals, and straightforward completions, and attach the same-week concept-tagged exit-ticket result where the anonymous linkage permits. I still need Ridgeway to confirm the roster mapping and the first-week export before I promise that join.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: And I don't want the ID linkage to become an afterthought once April starts. Before we leave this, I need Ridgeway to confirm that each of the three classes can use the same stable anonymous student ID across the tutor export and the weekly exit tickets starting in the first week. Otherwise, that really- it changes what we can claim from the pilot.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Agreed. I’ll treat that as a gating dependency rather than an implementation detail: no linked exit-ticket analysis unless Ridgeway confirms a stable class-consistent anonymous ID and the week-one export. I can still retain aggregate, de-identified interaction summaries if that slips, but they answer a much narrower question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: I’ll contact the Ridgeway algebra teachers too, just to confirm the weekly exit-ticket timing can stay consistent with their April unit sequence. There’s no value in getting a technically clean join if the prompt lands before they’ve taught the relevant, uh, idea. But the stable ID and week-one export are the gate for the student-level claims.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Agreed. I’ll hold the linkage-dependent configuration behind that confirmation, and otherwise keep the April telemetry export de-identified and usable at the aggregate level. Once Elena has the teachers’ timing check and Ridgeway confirms the mapping, I can lock the event schema and the graduated-hint instrumentation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should stop there rather than rush the rest. We can pick it up once we have those Ridgeway— once we have those confirmations from Ridgeway. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Sounds good. Bye, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Thanks, take care.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. We're getting into a really practical stretch here, so I'm hoping we can leave today with a launch routine a teacher can actually use while teaching, not like a second job, and a clear picture of what students see on day one. Before we get into that, has anyone heard anything new from Ridgeway about device or network readiness?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: I have two readiness items, though Ridgeway has not confirmed them yet. We need a full-class simultaneous-login test, including the transition between problem pages, and confirmation that filtering permits both the tutor domain and the authentication callback; in staging, two Chromebook models pause noticeably after the first hint panel despite normal server latency. Also, a routine privacy update: student-level logs cannot leave the school during the pilot, so vendor reporting is limited to weekly classroom-level aggregates.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Hm, that’s a concern.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: That changes what we can reasonably ask teachers to do with the review card, at least during the pilot. Arun, with the live class view, what would a teacher actually see, if anything? I’d strongly prefer a simple status or a short flag list after class, not something that has them monitoring thirty individual screens while they’re teaching.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: I'd make it strictly non-live. At most, teachers get an after-class list, and during the period they see classroom-level status, like sign-in completion and any system outage, not individual student traces. Given the privacy constraint, the review card can't carry persistent student linkage anyway, so I wouldn't, wouldn't imply teachers should intervene from it in real time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: I think non-live is important. If students think a teacher is watching their hint use moment to moment, that changes the behavior we’re trying to understand, and it probably makes asking for help feel more exposing. For day one, could the teacher just frame it as a private practice tool, using the same brief language across all three classes, and then…

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: I like a common script, but I’d avoid calling it fully private if the school still has the usual educational records around it. Something like, this is practice, nobody is watching your choices as you work, and the point is to try a path, use help when you need it, and keep your reasoning on paper. Nia, does that persistence language land okay with seventh graders, or does it start to sound evaluative?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. I’d make the first sentence even less about persistence. Something like, “Getting stuck is a normal part of learning algebra, and the help options are there for different moments.” Then the paper-reasoning piece can follow, because otherwise some students may hear “keep trying” as, you know, don’t ask for help yet.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Exactly. I'd say, “Start with what you think, and choose the kind of help that fits where you are,” rather than treating waiting for a hint as the virtue. Then we should be explicit that a hint isn't- that it isn't an answer key. It may ask them to look back at their equation or their representation, and they should keep that work on paper.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: I can configure the hint labels and the first-use prompt to match that, so there’s no language that treats escalation as failure. Elena, operationally, where in a normal algebra period is the least disruptive place for the teacher to pause after students first encounter a hint and, uh, reframe it if needed? I don’t want April’s onboarding flow to become a separate routine.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: It belongs right after the first problem, not as a separate stop. Once most students have opened a hint, the teacher can take maybe thirty seconds and say, “Notice what kind of help you chose. Write the next step you’re trying,” then keep circulating. I do need to check the teachers’ pacing, though. If their first topics are, um, not lined up, we may need a launch task with the same algebraic structure rather than identical content.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: That works technically. We can use the first problem as a common onboarding shell, with the same hint behavior and the same 30-second reframe, while the actual item comes from each class's current sequence. Before we settle the sign-in steps, I still need Ridgeway to verify whether the managed Chromebooks keep browser sessions across bells and cart swaps. Otherwise, that first-problem pause could turn into repeated authentication interruptions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: And that’s why I don’t want the teacher owning authentication on day one. Could Ridgeway have a tech aide or someone from the library on call for that first session? The teacher can have a very simple fallback—keep working the problem on paper, don’t keep refreshing, and we’ll resume when the connection returns. I’ll check the pacing question with the three teachers at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Could we be careful about what the stalled-session message says? If a student comes back after a drop and it looks like their work vanished, they may think they did something wrong. Arun, do you know what they’ll actually see on authentication failure or when they resume? Maybe the fallback language can, um, reassure them that their paper work still counts and they can pick up where they left off.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: On an authentication failure, they get a neutral reconnect screen. It doesn't suggest they got an answer wrong, and any work the server confirmed picks up at the last saved state. I should check exactly what happens to local drafts on those Chromebooks before I promise that, especially if the hint panel stalls. We can say, "Your paper work is still useful. Wait for the reconnect prompt instead of refreshing," because that's safer than saying nothing can be lost.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: That feels right—paper is the fallback, not a punishment when the technology fails. For the teacher orientation, I’d give them exactly that one line and a card for who to contact, rather than asking them to, um, diagnose reconnect screens while they’re trying to launch algebra. Arun, once you’ve checked the local-draft behavior, can we rehearse the actual student-facing wording in the simultaneous-login test?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: That’s the right place to test it. I’ll verify the resume and local-draft behavior on both Chromebook models before the full-class check, then we can walk through the exact reconnect wording with a student account. And if the draft is- if it isn’t durable, the message needs to be much more conservative.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: That sounds good. I’d like the first use to feel low-stakes, too, so a reconnect or a hint that comes at an odd time doesn’t become evidence, in their minds, that they’re bad at this. Elena, after that first problem, is there room for a very quick anonymous check, just whether the tutor felt clear to use, or is even that too much for the teachers’ pacing?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Mm, potentially, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: I think there is room, if it’s literally one anonymous mark as students close the first problem, clear to use, somewhat clear, not clear yet. But I’d keep it separate from the math exit ticket and only do it that first day. Otherwise it starts becoming another, another little procedure the teachers have to manage.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: That seems workable as long as it stays genuinely anonymous and doesn't go into the tutor. A paper slip or a simple three-option mark avoids creating another student-level record under the current restriction. We can give teachers the exact one-line instruction in the orientation, along with the reconnect fallback.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Okay, just the first day.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Good, I’ll fold that into a compact orientation with the first-problem reframe, the reconnect fallback, and that single anonymous clarity check. The remaining thing I need from Ridgeway is the teachers’ April sequence. I don’t want us promising a common first task before we know whether the algebraic structure can genuinely align across all three rooms.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: One operational caveat: with the privacy office’s restriction, the planned student-level linkage from tutor traces to exit tickets is not available during this pilot; platform exports will have no persistent identifiers. I’ll revise the export and storage configuration accordingly, so we are not building the orientation around a review workflow we cannot actually support.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Yeah. That is a real limitation, and we should say it plainly in the orientation: this is not a teacher monitoring system, and we’re not asking them to act on individual usage. For the pilot, I’m still comfortable learning from the classroom observations, the common exit tickets, and how the launch actually holds up—but I don’t want anyone implying we can make student-level claims from aggregate exports.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Yes—and that framing should help students feel safer using help, not watched for it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Before we close, I want the orientation to say that directly, not as fine print. Teachers teach, students use the help options, and technical trouble goes to the support contact. I’ll confirm the three pacing sequences and whether we can use that common onboarding structure. Then we can keep the teacher session short and grounded in those two or three actual classroom moments.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: I’ll send the revised, identifier-free export specification and the preflight checklist for the simultaneous-login, filter, and Chromebook resume tests. Once Elena has the sequences, the onboarding shell itself is ready. The one thing we shouldn’t treat as settled is the common first-task content, since that still—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Rodriguez
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should stop there. Arun has the preflight pieces, and I’ll get the pacing check back from Ridgeway. We can pick up the first-task content next time. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Nia Okafor
transcript.text: Thanks, everyone. Talk soon.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Arun Mehta
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye.
